articles.body: Gotenberg's API has no UI signal, so body and header evidence matter Gotenberg is an API service for document conversion. Its root route says that it has no UI and directs users to the API documentation. That design changes the way an exposure measurement should be read: a public Gotenberg service may look like a sparse web page even when it can process files and fetch remote URLs. The fixed measurement on November 23, 2026 returned 3,971 matches for app="Gotenberg" , eight for title="Gotenberg" , and 341,954 for http.body="Gotenberg" . The scope was sub_type=all , page 1, page size 1. The body count is broad and includes documentation, source pages, logs, and articles, so it is not a count of conversion services.

articles.excerpt: AI disclosure: I wrote this article with AI assistance (Claude). The code comes from a small crawler we maintain, and I got every number in the output sections by running it locally on 2026-11-22. Mos…
articles.body: AI disclosure: I wrote this article with AI assistance (Claude). The code comes from a small crawler we maintain, and I got every number in the output sections by running it locally on 2026-11-22. Most RAG pipelines start with "get the docs into the vector store", and that step often turns out worse than it should. Raw HTML is full of navigation menus, cookie banners, "Edit this page" links and footers. If you embed all of that, every chunk carries the same boilerplate, retrieval gets noisy, and you pay for tokens that add nothing. People often reach for a headless browser first. For a large share of the web, including most documentation sites, blogs and help centers, you don't need one. The HTML the server sends already contains the content.

articles.body: Software engineering teams rarely lose hours solely on writing business logic. Instead, productivity bleeds out through small, recurring friction points: waiting for manual pull request reviews, testing builds across environments one by one, discovering security vulnerabilities after deployment, and executing manual release scripts. None of these tasks require active human supervision, yet engineering teams routinely defer automating them because it feels like low-priority infrastructure work. Implementing a few fundamental GitHub Actions workflows can automate these operational chores and give your team hours of focused time back every week. 1.

articles.body: Before this migration, here was the state of my Kubernetes platform: 7 Helm releases running on AWS EKS — kube-prometheus-stack, Tempo, Loki, Promtail, Chaos Mesh, plus the microservices overlay Each installed manually with helm install or kubectl apply -k from my laptop No drift detection: if a resource was patched directly in the cluster, I'd find out when something broke No audit trail: the deployment history was a mix of terminal history and my own memory Deployment ordering enforced by me running commands in the right sequence This is how most Kubernetes platforms look after the "it works" phase. The cluster is functional but fragile. The state of your infrastructure lives in your head, not in git.

articles.title: Your 20% Code Stacked on Your Sale Price. You Just Sold Below Cost.
articles.excerpt: Nobody set that price, and customers are paying it You marked a product down for Black Friday. Compare-at price $50, sale price $39.99 — a clean, planned margin. Separately, you created a storewide co…
articles.body: Nobody set that price, and customers are paying it You marked a product down for Black Friday. Compare-at price $50, sale price $39.99 — a clean, planned margin. Separately, you created a storewide code: BFCM20, 20% off, the one in your ads and your email header. What you did not plan is that on most store setups, the code applies on top of the sale price by default. $39.99 minus 20% is $31.99. If your landed cost — product, shipping, fees — is $33, you are now paying customers a small fee for the privilege of fulfilling their orders, at your highest volume of the year.

articles.body: SpaceX launched a batch of classified satellites this morning (Nov. 22), on the NROL-136 mission out of California. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California). It was the sixth National Reconnaissance Office launch (NROL) this year to deliver a payload, or group of payloads, to low Earth orbit , all which have been carried out by SpaceX 's workhorse Falcon 9. The launch marks another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov.22, 1989: NASA launches space shuttle Discovery on classified STS-33 mission for the US military
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night. This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military launched several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites . The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified. articles.body: On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part.
